turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me, I really appreciate it. Um, I hope I'm not wasting your time—it's probably just a little quirk, really. But, well, I guess what brought me in is that I've been having a bit of trouble just... staying in my chair? 

Like, during staff meetings at the school where I teach, or even just sitting down for dinner, I'll suddenly get up when everyone else is seated. I always try to make myself useful, you know, like I'll pop up to refill the coffee, or go check on a handout, or just walk to the back of the room. But I guess I do it even when nothing is really urgent. My family sort of gently pointed it out, so I thought I should ask a professional about it. 

Is that... is that the sort of thing you can help with? I just want to make sure I'm in the right place and explaining it okay.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they have trouble staying in their chair and frequently get up during meetings or dinners when remaining seated is expected.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting down and feel the urge to get up, does it feel more like your body just can't stay still and needs to move, or does it feel more like you're anxious or uncomfortable and getting up helps calm you down?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... I don't think it's anxiety. I really hope I don't come across as a nervous person! I think it's more just... my body just sort of expects to be doing something? If that makes sense? 

It's like I just have this momentum. Especially lately. Since the house got a lot quieter after my youngest left for college, I just... I keep busy. I'll move straight from lesson planning to throwing in a load of laundry, then I'm off to help with softball practice, and then I'm chopping food for a community event... just without much of a pause at all. 

I always tell myself it's just being productive and helpful, you know? But even on nights when I promised myself I would finally just sit down and rest... I just keep going. I just don't seem to stop. Is it okay that I'm explaining it like this? I just want to make sure I'm answering your question properly.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes having constant momentum, moving from task to task without pause, and being unable to stop even when promising herself to rest, which aligns with being 'on the go' or 'driven by a motor'.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies that her urge to move is driven by anxiety or nervousness.

turns.doctor_question: Have you always been someone who needs to stay busy and active like this, even going back to when you were a child or teenager? Or is this something that's gotten noticeably worse recently?
turns.patient_response:
Well, um... I suppose I've always been a bit of a busy bee, really. I hope that's alright to say. My mother, bless her, she used to joke that I wore a path right into the floorboards between my desk and the pencil sharpener before I was even ten years old. I just liked to make sure my pencils were perfectly sharp, you know? 

And, um, I think my teachers back then... well, they were very kind, but my report cards usually said I was bright—which was nice of them to say!—but that I maybe had a little trouble staying in my seat or waiting my turn to speak. I was just so eager to participate, I think. 

So it's not entirely new, no. It's just... maybe it stands out a bit more now that I don't have the kids at home to chase after. Does that make sense? I hope I'm not overcomplicating things.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions having trouble staying in her seat and constantly getting up to sharpen pencils during childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes herself as having always been a 'busy bee' who stays active.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient explicitly notes that her childhood report cards mentioned she had trouble waiting her turn to speak.

turns.doctor_question: When you're going through these busy periods where you're constantly moving from one thing to another, how many hours of sleep are you actually getting at night? And do you feel rested, or do you feel like you need more sleep?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, sleep... well, I sleep just fine, I think! I hope I didn't give the impression that I'm up all night. I really try to get a good night's rest, usually about six or seven hours, which I think is pretty normal for someone my age? 

I mean, sometimes I might wake up a little early and just decide to start the day, maybe get a head start on grading papers or something, but I don't feel exhausted or anything. I actually feel quite rested. I certainly don't feel like I'm running on empty. 

I just... I like to make the most of my day, you know? Is six or seven hours alright? I hope that doesn't sound like I'm neglecting my health.

symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient states they 'sleep just fine' and get a good night's rest, denying significant sleep disturbances.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient explicitly denies feeling exhausted or running on empty, noting they feel quite rested.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient denies a decreased need for sleep, stating they get a normal six to seven hours of sleep rather than staying up all night.

turns.doctor_question: When you're in conversations or meetings, do you find yourself interrupting others or blurting things out before they've finished speaking? Or do you tend to think before you speak?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, well... I do try my very best to be polite, I really do. But, um... sometimes I suppose I might get just a little bit ahead of myself? I hope that doesn't make me sound rude. 

It's just that, especially in group discussions—like at my book club or during our curriculum meetings at school—someone will be talking, and the response just sort of... forms in my head so quickly. And before I can even remind myself to wait, I've already jumped in and blurted it out. 

I don't mean to cut anyone off, I promise! I just get so engaged in the conversation, and I want to contribute, and it just slips out before they've quite finished their thought. I always feel a bit terribly about it afterward. Is that... is that the sort of thing you mean? I hope you don't think I'm a terrible listener.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they often blurt out responses before others have finished their thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient admits to jumping into conversations and cutting people off during group discussions like book clubs and meetings.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned feeling a bit terribly about interrupting people at book club and your curriculum meetings. Has this habit of interrupting or blurting things out caused any real problems for you—like affecting your relationships with colleagues or friends, or impacting how people perceive you professionally?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, well... I wouldn't say they are *real* problems, exactly. I mean, I certainly hope they don't think badly of me! But... I suppose, if I'm being completely honest with you—and I do want to make sure I'm giving you all the right information—it has started to affect my relationships just a little bit. At work, and in my community. 

I've started to notice that people... well, they seem to lose patience with me sometimes during our curriculum meetings and at book club. I can see it in their faces or when they sigh after I've jumped in too quickly. And instead of enjoying the discussion and feeling connected to everyone, I just end up leaving feeling terribly embarrassed about it all. 

I really do try my best to be a good colleague and a good friend, I promise. Does that make sense? I just hope I haven't completely ruined their impression of me. Do you think that's something I can fix if I just try a little harder to be quiet?

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient acknowledges the doctor's premise about their habit of blurting things out, noting that people lose patience when they have 'jumped in too quickly.'
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient confirms that their habit of interrupting others during conversations at book club and curriculum meetings is negatively affecting their relationships.

turns.patient_response:
Oh, well... goodness, I think my attention is actually quite good! I really do. I mean, as a teacher, you simply have to be able to focus, don't you? 

When I'm grading papers or reading for my book club, I... well, I don't think my mind wanders terribly much. I try very hard to stay on task. It's really more of a... a physical restlessness, I suppose? Like my body just wants to be doing something, even if my brain is perfectly happy looking at an essay.
